4.name: Afghanistan
4.fato: A crossroads of the Silk Road, it was invaded by Alexander, the Mongols and the British, who failed to subdue it. The Soviet invasion of 1979 brought ten years of war and the rise of the mujahideen. After a civil war, the Taliban took power in 1996; the American invasion of 2001 toppled them, but they returned in 2021 with the US withdrawal, after twenty years of occupation.

8.name: Albania
8.fato: Heir to the Illyrians, it resisted the Ottomans under Skanderbeg in the 15th century before being absorbed for four centuries. Independent in 1912. Under Enver Hoxha, from 1944 to 1985, it became the most isolated state in Europe, atheist by decree and covered in bunkers. Its opening in 1991 was followed by economic collapse in 1997.

10.name: Antarctica
10.fato: Set aside for science and peace by the Antarctic Treaty of 1959.

12.name: Algeria
12.fato: It was an Ottoman province and the base of the Barbary corsairs of Algiers. France conquered it in 1830 and treated it as part of its own territory, with a million settlers. The war of independence, from 1954 to 1962, killed hundreds of thousands and brought down the French Fourth Republic. In the 1990s it went through a civil war with Islamists that left about 200,000 dead.

20.name: Andorra
al: Principality of the Valleys of Andorra
20.fato: According to tradition, it owes its autonomy to Charlemagne. Since 1278 it has been ruled by two co-princes — the Bishop of Urgell and, today, the President of France — a feudal arrangement that survived intact. It stayed neutral in both world wars and only adopted a modern constitution in 1993. It lives off mountain tourism and trade.

24.name: Angola
24.fato: The Kingdom of Kongo established diplomatic relations with Portugal in 1483, before the region became the largest supplier of enslaved people to Brazil. The war of independence began in 1961 and ended in 1975, immediately followed by a civil war between the MPLA and UNITA that lasted until 2002, fueled by the Cold War, oil and diamonds.

28.name: Antigua and Barbuda
28.fato: English Harbour was a British naval base in the Caribbean, commanded by Nelson. A sugar economy built on enslaved labor until abolition in 1834. Independent in 1981. Today it lives almost entirely off tourism, and has more registered vessels than inhabitants.

31.name: Azerbaijan
31.fato: Baku had the first oil wells exploited industrially, in the 19th century, and at one point produced half of the world's oil. Majority Shia but with a secular state, it was Soviet from 1920 to 1991. The conflict with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh spanned three decades, with wars in 1988–94 and 2020 and the full recapture of the region in 2023.

32.name: Argentina
32.fato: Independent from Spain in 1816, it consolidated after civil wars between unitarians and federalists. Between 1880 and 1930 it received one of the largest European migrations in the world, which reshaped its population. Peronism, from 1946 on, has marked its politics to this day. The 1976–83 dictatorship left about 30,000 disappeared and ended after the defeat in the Falklands.

36.name: Australia
36.fato: Inhabited by Aboriginal peoples for more than 50,000 years, with the oldest continuous culture in the world. It began as a British penal colony in 1788; colonization devastated native populations. It federated in 1901 but kept the White Australia policy until the 1970s. Aboriginal people were only counted in the census from 1967, and the official apology came in 2008.

40.name: Austria
40.fato: Heartland of the Habsburgs, who for six centuries ruled much of central Europe. The Austro-Hungarian Empire brought together twelve peoples and collapsed in 1918, at the end of World War I. Annexed by Hitler in 1938, it was occupied by the Allies until 1955, when it regained sovereignty under a commitment to neutrality. In the early 20th century Vienna was a cultural capital of music and thought.

44.name: The Bahamas
44.fato: A pirate base in the 18th century, Blackbeard included, until the British crackdown. It took in American loyalists and the people they enslaved after 1783. It prospered from smuggling during American Prohibition. Independent in 1973, it lives off tourism and financial services.

48.name: Bahrain
48.fato: It was the center of the ancient Dilmun civilization, a trading post between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley. The first Gulf country to extract oil, in 1932, and also the first to see its reserves run out, shifting to finance. Independent in 1971. Its Shia majority under a Sunni monarchy led to protests in 2011, crushed with Saudi support.

50.name: Bangladesh
50.fato: It was East Bengal, a region famous for its weaving before British industrialization. It joined Pakistan in 1947, but the repression of the Bengali language and culture led to the 1971 liberation war, with Indian support and a documented genocide. It suffered devastating cyclones and famine. It sharply reduced poverty with microcredit and the textile industry, despite its climate vulnerability.

51.name: Armenia
51.fato: It adopted Christianity as its state religion in 301, the first state in the world to do so, and created its own alphabet in 405. Divided among empires for centuries. About 1.5 million Armenians were killed in the Ottoman genocide of 1915, which scattered its diaspora across the world. Independent from the USSR in 1991, it disputes Nagorno-Karabakh with Azerbaijan.

52.name: Barbados
52.fato: An English colony from 1627, it pioneered the sugar plantation model with enslaved labor that spread across the Caribbean. It had the island's largest slave revolt in 1816. Independent in 1966, it kept a democratic stability rare in the region and became a republic in 2021, leaving the British monarchy.

56.name: Belgium
56.fato: Ruled by the Spanish, Austrians, French and Dutch, it became independent in 1830 as a buffer state between powers. It was the second country in Europe to industrialize. Under Leopold II, it exploited the Congo as the king's personal property, in a regime of extreme violence. Invaded in both world wars, today it is federal, split between Flemings and Walloons, and hosts the institutions of the European Union.

60.name: Bermuda
60.fato: An English colony since 1609, after an accidental shipwreck.

64.name: Bhutan
64.fato: A Buddhist kingdom unified in the 17th century, it stayed isolated by choice, without roads or currency until the 1960s. In 1972 it adopted Gross National Happiness as its measure of progress. Television only arrived in 1999. It went from absolute to constitutional monarchy in 2008, at the king's own initiative. It is the only country in the world with a negative carbon balance.

68.name: Bolivia
68.fato: The Cerro Rico of Potosí sustained the Spanish Empire with its silver, at the cost of countless Indigenous lives. Independent in 1825, it lost its access to the sea in the War of the Pacific and territory in the Chaco War. The 1952 revolution nationalized the mines and gave Indigenous people the vote. In 2006 it elected Evo Morales, its first Indigenous president.

70.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
70.fato: A medieval kingdom in its own right, it was Ottoman for four centuries, which explains its Muslim majority. The Sarajevo assassination of 1914 triggered World War I. The 1992–95 war brought ethnic cleansing, the siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica massacre. The Dayton Agreement ended the conflict by creating a state divided into two entities.

72.name: Botswana
72.fato: As the British protectorate of Bechuanaland, it was one of the poorest countries in the world when it became independent in 1966. The discovery of diamonds the following year, combined with stable institutions and prudent management of the revenue, produced decades of growth — a rare case of a natural resource that did not become a curse. The Okavango is its great natural treasure.

76.name: Brazil
76.fato: Home to hundreds of Indigenous peoples, it was a Portuguese colony from 1500, driven by brazilwood, sugar and gold with enslaved African labor. Seat of the Portuguese court in 1808, it became an independent empire in 1822 and a republic in 1889, a year after abolishing slavery — the last country in the Americas to do so. It lived under military dictatorship from 1964 to 1985. Brasília, inaugurated in 1960, was built from scratch in the cerrado.

84.name: Belize
84.fato: Colonized by the English, who extracted logwood, it was British Honduras until 1973 and independent in 1981. The only Central American country with English as its official language. Guatemala claimed its territory for decades. It holds part of the second-largest barrier reef in the world and important Maya sites.

90.name: Solomon Islands
90.fato: Scene of the Battle of Guadalcanal, one of the turning points of the Pacific War, in 1942. A British protectorate, independent in 1978. It went through ethnic conflict between 1998 and 2003, ended by a regional mission led by Australia. It depends on timber, fishing and foreign aid.

92.name: British Virgin Islands
al: Virgin Islands of the United Kingdom

96.name: Brunei
al: Nation of Brunei, the Abode of Peace
96.fato: The sultanate ruled much of Borneo and the Philippines in the 16th century before shrinking in the face of Europeans and pirates. A British protectorate from 1888 to 1984. The discovery of oil in 1929 gave it one of the highest per capita incomes in Asia, with no income tax. The same dynasty has ruled for more than six centuries.

100.name: Bulgaria
100.fato: The First Bulgarian Empire, in the 9th century, adopted Christianity and the Cyrillic alphabet, spreading it across the Slavic world. It spent five centuries under Ottoman rule, until independence in 1878. Allied with Germany in both wars, it became a Soviet satellite in 1946. It saved its 48,000 Jews from deportation during World War II, a rare case in occupied Europe.

104.name: Myanmar
al: Republic of the Union of Myanmar
104.fato: Bagan has thousands of temples built between the 11th and 13th centuries. A powerful kingdom until three wars against the British folded it into colonial India. Independent in 1948, it lived under military juntas from 1962. Aung San Suu Kyi led the opposition for decades; the brief opening was cut short by the 2021 coup. The persecution of the Rohingya caused a mass exodus in 2017.

108.name: Burundi
108.fato: It shares with Rwanda the history of its kingdoms and the Hutu–Tutsi divide deepened by Belgian colonization. Independent in 1962, it suffered massacres in 1972 and 1993 and a civil war that only ended in 2005. It remains among the poorest countries in the world, heavily dependent on coffee.

112.name: Belarus
112.fato: Part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and then of the Russian Empire, it was the territory most devastated by World War II: it lost about a quarter of its population and almost its entire Jewish community. Chernobyl, in 1986, contaminated much of its soil. Independent in 1991, it has been ruled by Lukashenko since 1994, in the longest-lasting regime in Europe.

116.name: Cambodia
116.fato: Angkor was the largest preindustrial city in the world, capital of an empire that dominated Southeast Asia between the 9th and 15th centuries. A French protectorate, independent in 1953. The Khmer Rouge regime, between 1975 and 1979, killed about a quarter of the population in labor camps and executions, until it was overthrown by a Vietnamese invasion.

120.name: Cameroon
120.fato: A German colony, it was split between France and the United Kingdom after World War I — a division that still fuels conflict with the English-speaking minority, in armed crisis since 2017. Independent in 1960. Paul Biya has been in power since 1982. Its geographic diversity earned it the nickname "Africa in miniature".

124.name: Canada
124.fato: Fought over by France and England, it became British in 1763 — hence the persistence of French in Quebec. The confederation of 1867 united the provinces, but the constitutional ties with London were only cut in 1982. It built a transcontinental railway to settle the west. Since the 1990s it has been reckoning with the legacy of the residential schools for Indigenous children.

132.name: Cape Verde
132.fato: An uninhabited archipelago until the Portuguese arrived in 1460, it became a hub of the Atlantic slave trade and a meeting point of African and European cultures, which gave rise to Creole and to morna. Independent in 1975. With no natural resources and historic droughts, it bet on democratic stability, education and tourism.

136.name: Cayman Islands
136.fato: It became one of the largest offshore financial centers in the world.

140.name: Central African Republic
140.fato: Exploited by French concession companies with forced labor. Independent in 1960. Bokassa seized power in a coup and crowned himself emperor in 1977, in a ceremony that consumed much of the national budget. Since 2012 it has been torn by conflict between militias, despite its wealth in diamonds, gold and uranium.

144.name: Sri Lanka
al: Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka
144.fato: Anuradhapura was a Buddhist capital for more than a thousand years. The Portuguese, Dutch and British fought over the island for the spice trade and later for tea. Independent in 1948. The civil war between the Sinhalese government and the Tamil Tigers lasted from 1983 to 2009, with about 100,000 dead. It was hit by the 2004 tsunami and the economic collapse of 2022.

148.name: Chad
148.fato: For centuries it linked the Sahel to the trans-Saharan routes, with the Kanem–Bornu Empire. Independent from France in 1960, it went through decades of civil war and conflict with Libya over the Aouzou Strip. Lake Chad, which sustained millions, has shrunk by more than 90% since the 1960s, worsening disputes and displacement.

152.name: Chile
152.fato: Independent in 1818, it expanded north in the War of the Pacific (1879–83), taking territory rich in saltpeter and copper from Peru and Bolivia. Allende's socialist government was overthrown by Pinochet's coup in 1973, which ushered in seventeen years of dictatorship and radical free-market reforms. It returned to democracy in 1990.

156.name: China
156.fato: Unified in 221 BC under Qin Shi Huang, it alternated between dynasties and fragmentation for two millennia, inventing paper, gunpowder, the compass and printing. The Opium Wars, in the 19th century, forced the country open and began the "century of humiliation". The republic of 1911 overthrew the last dynasty; after civil war and Japanese invasion, Mao proclaimed the People's Republic in 1949. Deng's reforms, from 1978, turned it into the world's second-largest economy.

158.name: Taiwan
158.fato: Inhabited by Austronesian peoples, it was Dutch, then Chinese, and a Japanese colony from 1895 to 1945. In 1949 the Nationalist government defeated by Mao took refuge here, keeping the Republic of China. It lived under martial law until 1987 and democratized in the 1990s. It became a linchpin of the world economy by producing most of the advanced semiconductors.

170.name: Colombia
170.fato: Bogotá was the seat of the Viceroyalty of New Granada. Independent with Bolívar, it was part of Gran Colombia until 1831. It lost Panama in 1903 with American support for separatism. It lived through La Violencia in the 1940s–50s and, from 1964, an armed conflict with guerrillas and cartels that lasted over fifty years, with a peace agreement with the FARC in 2016.

174.name: Comoros
174.fato: A crossroads of Arab, Persian and African routes in the Mozambique Channel. Independent from France in 1975, except Mayotte, which chose to remain French. It has had more than twenty coups or attempts since then, several involving the French mercenary Bob Denard. It is one of the world's largest producers of ylang-ylang, used in perfumery.

175.name: Mayotte
175.fato: It chose by referendum to remain French when the Comoros broke away.

178.name: Republic of the Congo
178.fato: Brazzaville was the capital of French Equatorial Africa and the seat of Free France during World War II. Independent in 1960, it adopted Marxism in the 1970s. It went through civil war between 1997 and 1999. It depends almost entirely on offshore oil, and holds part of the second-largest rainforest in the world.

180.name: DR Congo
180.fato: It was the personal property of King Leopold II of Belgium from 1885 to 1908, under a forced-labor regime that killed millions. Independent in 1960, it plunged into crisis with the secession of Katanga and the assassination of Lumumba. Mobutu ruled for 32 years. The Congo Wars, between 1996 and 2003, drew in nine countries and killed millions — the deadliest conflict since 1945.

188.name: Costa Rica
188.fato: A poor, peripheral colony, which limited the concentration of land and favored small landowners. After a brief civil war, it abolished its armed forces in 1948 and moved the military budget to education and health. It built the most stable democracy in the region and became a world reference in environmental conservation, with a quarter of its territory protected.

191.name: Croatia
191.fato: Tied to Hungary from 1102 and later to the Habsburgs, it served as a military frontier against the Ottomans. It joined Yugoslavia in 1918. It declared independence in 1991, which set off four years of war with local Serbs and the Yugoslav Army, with cities like Vukovar razed. It joined the European Union in 2013.

192.name: Cuba
192.fato: Spain's last colony in the Americas, it became independent in 1898 under American tutelage. The 1959 revolution brought Fidel Castro to power and aligned the country with the USSR, leading to the Bay of Pigs invasion and the 1962 Missile Crisis, the closest the world has come to nuclear war. It has been under a US embargo since 1962.

196.name: Cyprus
196.fato: Crossed by Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Venetians and Ottomans, it became British in 1878. Independent in 1960, it saw tension between Greek and Turkish Cypriots explode with the 1974 coup and the Turkish invasion that followed, which split the island in two. Its capital, Nicosia, is the last divided capital in Europe.

203.name: Czechia
203.fato: Bohemia was a center of the Holy Roman Empire and the scene of the Defenestration of Prague, which set off the Thirty Years' War. Independent from Austria-Hungary in 1918, it was occupied by Hitler in 1938 and by Soviet tanks in 1968, crushing the Prague Spring. The Velvet Revolution brought down communism in 1989, and the split from Slovakia in 1993 was negotiated without violence.

204.name: Benin
204.fato: The Kingdom of Dahomey grew rich on the Atlantic slave trade from the port of Ouidah, and had an all-female military corps feared by Europeans. A French colony in 1894, independent in 1960. It lived under a Marxist-Leninist regime from 1975 to 1990, and was one of the first African countries to make a peaceful democratic transition.

208.name: Denmark
208.fato: Center of the Viking empire that once ruled England, it was for centuries the dominant power of the north. Its flag, from 1219, is the oldest still in use. It lost Norway in 1814 and German territories in 1864. Occupied by the Nazis, it managed to save almost all of its Jews in 1943. Greenland and the Faroe Islands remain under its Crown.

212.name: Dominica
212.fato: The last stronghold of the Carib people, who resisted colonization for centuries thanks to the mountainous terrain — a Carib territory still exists on the island. It alternated between France and England. Independent in 1978. It was devastated by Hurricane Maria in 2017 and is trying to become the first climate-resilient country.

214.name: Dominican Republic
214.fato: Santo Domingo was the first permanent European settlement in the Americas, in 1496. Independent from Spain, and then from Haiti in 1844, it lived under Trujillo's dictatorship for thirty years, marked by the massacre of Haitians in 1937. It suffered an American intervention in 1965. Today it has one of the most dynamic economies in the Caribbean.

218.name: Ecuador
218.fato: Part of the Inca Empire and then of Bolívar's Gran Colombia, it broke away in 1830. It lived off cocoa and later bananas and Amazonian oil. It had a long border dispute with Peru, only settled in 1998. The Galápagos Islands, where Darwin collected data in 1835, shaped the theory of evolution. It adopted the US dollar in 2000.

222.name: El Salvador
222.fato: Land of the Pipil people, it was conquered by the Spanish in 1524. An economy dominated by coffee and a few families fed the peasant uprising of 1932, crushed with thousands dead. The 1980–92 civil war killed 75,000 people. After the war it faced an epidemic of gang violence and made bitcoin legal tender in 2021.

226.name: Equatorial Guinea
226.fato: The only African nation with Spanish as an official language, it was a Spanish colony until 1968. Macías Nguema set up a regime that killed or exiled much of the population, until he was deposed by his nephew in 1979 — who has ruled ever since, the longest-serving head of state in the world. Oil discovered in the 1990s enriched the elite.

231.name: Ethiopia
231.fato: One of the oldest states in the world, with the Kingdom of Aksum and Christianity since the 4th century. It was never colonized: it defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, becoming a symbol of Pan-Africanism. Briefly occupied by Mussolini between 1936 and 1941. Emperor Haile Selassie fell in 1974, followed by the Derg regime and the famine of the 1980s. It uses its own thirteen-month calendar.

232.name: Eritrea
232.fato: An Italian colony from 1890, it was federated with Ethiopia in 1952 and annexed in 1962, which began thirty years of war of independence, won in 1991 and formalized in 1993. A new border war with Ethiopia, from 1998 to 2000, killed tens of thousands. It has lived under one-party rule since its founding.

233.name: Estonia
233.fato: Forcibly Christianized by German crusaders in the 13th century, it passed through Danish, Swedish and Russian hands. Independent in 1918 and re-annexed by the USSR in 1940. It regained sovereignty in 1991 without bloodshed, through the Singing Revolution. It became a world reference in digital government, with internet voting since 2005.

234.name: Faroe Islands
234.fato: Islands settled by Norsemen around the year 800.

238.name: Falkland Islands
238.fato: The target of the Falklands War between Argentina and the United Kingdom, in 1982.

239.name: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands
al: South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands

242.name: Fiji
242.fato: A meeting point of Melanesian and Polynesian routes, it was a British colony that brought in Indian workers for the sugarcane plantations — today about 40% of the population. Independent in 1970, it has had four coups since 1987, largely tied to tension between Indigenous Fijians and Indo-Fijians.

246.name: Finland
246.fato: It was part of the Swedish kingdom for six centuries and a grand duchy of the Russian Empire for one. Independent in 1917, it resisted the Soviet invasion in the Winter War of 1939–40, losing territory but keeping its sovereignty. It maintained careful neutrality during the Cold War and only joined NATO in 2023, after the invasion of Ukraine.

250.name: France
250.fato: A centralized state since the Capetians, it reached the height of absolutism under Louis XIV. The Revolution of 1789 overthrew the monarchy and exported the idea of citizenship; Napoleon spread its civil code across Europe. It built the second-largest colonial empire in the world, lost between 1954 and 1962, above all in the traumatic Algerian War. Occupied by the Nazis in 1940, it later became one of the engines of European integration.

254.name: French Guiana
254.fato: Home to the European spaceport at Kourou.

258.name: French Polynesia
258.fato: It brings together 118 islands scattered over an area the size of Europe.

262.name: Djibouti
262.fato: French Somaliland until 1977, it owes its importance to its position on the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the gateway to the Red Sea. It hosts military bases of the United States, France, China and Japan in the same small territory. It serves as the main port for landlocked Ethiopia.

266.name: Gabon
266.fato: Libreville was founded to shelter enslaved people freed from a slave ship. A French colony, independent in 1960. Bongo and his son ruled for 55 years, until the 2023 coup. Oil gives it one of the highest per capita incomes in Africa, but poorly distributed. Almost 90% of its territory is covered by forest.

268.name: Georgia
268.fato: One of the first states to adopt Christianity, in the 4th century, it has its own alphabet and a language unrelated to its neighbors'. It had a golden age in the 12th century under Queen Tamar. Annexed by Russia in 1801 and Soviet from 1921. Independent in 1991, it lost control of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, and fought Russia in the 2008 war.

270.name: Gambia
270.fato: The narrowest country on the continent, shaped by the course of the Gambia River, which the British controlled to fight the slave trade. Independent in 1965. Jammeh ruled for 22 years and only left power in 2017 under regional military pressure after losing the election. It lives off tourism, peanuts and remittances.

275.name: Palestine
275.fato: Historic Palestine went from Ottoman rule to the British Mandate. The 1947 UN partition plan and the 1948 war brought the Nakba, with the expulsion or flight of about 700,000 Palestinians. The West Bank and Gaza were occupied in 1967. The PLO and the Oslo Accords created the Palestinian Authority in 1994, and the UN recognized it as an observer state in 2012.

276.name: Germany
276.fato: Fragmented into hundreds of principalities after the Thirty Years' War, it only became a single state in 1871, under Bismarck's Prussia. Defeated in 1918, it saw the Weimar Republic collapse and Nazism lead to the Holocaust and World War II. It was divided into two Germanys from 1949 to 1990, separated by the Berlin Wall from 1961. Reunified, it became the largest economy in Europe.

288.name: Ghana
288.fato: The Ashanti kingdom resisted the British in several wars in the 19th century. Its coast was lined with forts of the Atlantic slave trade, such as Elmina. In 1957 it became the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence, under Nkrumah, a leading figure of Pan-Africanism. After decades of coups, it built one of the most stable democracies on the continent.

292.name: Gibraltar
292.fato: Ceded to the United Kingdom by the Treaty of Utrecht, in 1713.

296.name: Kiribati
296.fato: The only country in all four hemispheres, spread over an ocean area larger than India. The British Gilbert Islands were the scene of the bloody Battle of Tarawa in 1943, and Kiritimati hosted British and American nuclear tests. Independent in 1979, it is among the most threatened by sea-level rise.

300.name: Greece
300.fato: Cradle of Athenian democracy, philosophy and Western theater in the 5th century BC. Conquered by Rome, it was for a thousand years the heart of the Byzantine Empire, until the fall of Constantinople in 1453. It freed itself from the Ottomans in 1832 after a war backed by European powers. It went through civil war and military dictatorship until 1974, and a devastating debt crisis from 2009.

304.name: Greenland
304.fato: The largest island in the world; an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark.

308.name: Grenada
308.fato: French and then British, it prospered on nutmeg and cocoa. Independent in 1974, it had a Marxist coup in 1979 and, after the execution of Prime Minister Maurice Bishop, was invaded by the United States in 1983. It has been democratically stable ever since.

312.name: Guadeloupe
312.fato: A French department in the Caribbean since 1946.

316.name: Guam
316.fato: A strategic US military base in the western Pacific.

320.name: Guatemala
320.fato: Heart of the Maya civilization, with Tikal among its most powerful centers. Independent in 1821. The CIA-backed coup of 1954, tied to United Fruit interests, began decades of instability and a 36-year civil war that killed 200,000 people, largely Indigenous, ended in 1996.

324.name: Guinea
324.fato: Part of its territory was home to the Mali and Songhai empires. It was the only territory to reject the French Community proposed by De Gaulle in 1958, and the French pulled out destroying what they could. Sékou Touré ruled until 1984 with harsh repression. It holds large bauxite reserves and was the epicenter of Ebola in 2014.

328.name: Guyana
328.fato: Colonized by the Dutch and then the British, who brought Indian workers after abolition — today half the population has that origin. Independent in 1966. It suffered the Jonestown massacre in 1978. It disputes the Essequibo region with Venezuela. The discovery of offshore oil in 2015 sent its economy soaring.

332.name: Haiti
332.fato: The slave revolt led by Toussaint Louverture defeated Napoleon's army and created, in 1804, the world's first Black republic. It was forced to pay France an indemnity, a debt that strangled it for more than a century. It endured American occupation, the Duvalier dictatorship and the 2010 earthquake, which killed more than 200,000 people.

334.name: Heard Island and McDonald Islands
al: Territory of Heard Island and McDonald Islands

336.name: Vatican City
336.fato: The Papal States ruled central Italy for a thousand years, until they were annexed in 1870. The pope declared himself a prisoner in the Vatican until the Lateran Treaty of 1929 created the current state — the smallest in the world. It holds St. Peter's Basilica, the Sistine Chapel and archives with centuries of documents.

340.name: Honduras
340.fato: Copán was an important Maya city. Independent in 1821, its economy was dominated by American banana companies in the early 20th century — hence the term "banana republic". It served as a base for the Nicaraguan Contras in the 1980s. It was hit by Hurricane Mitch in 1998 and a coup in 2009.

344.name: Hong Kong
al: Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China
344.fato: Handed back by the United Kingdom to China in 1997.

348.name: Hungary
348.fato: Founded by the Magyars in 896, it was devastated by the Mongols and later ruled by the Ottomans for 150 years. With Austria, it formed the dual empire in 1867. The Treaty of Trianon, in 1920, took two thirds of its territory and left millions of Hungarians outside its borders — a trauma still alive today. The 1956 uprising against the Soviets was crushed by tanks.

352.name: Iceland
352.fato: Settled by Norsemen around 870, in 930 it created the Althing, the oldest parliament still in operation. It was Danish until 1944, when it declared independence while Denmark was occupied. It fought the Cod Wars with the United Kingdom in the 1950s–70s. In 2008 its banking system collapsed spectacularly, and the country responded by prosecuting bankers.

356.name: India
356.fato: The Indus Valley civilization, from 2600 BC, is one of the oldest in the world. The Maurya, Gupta and Mughal empires shaped its culture before British rule, consolidated in 1858. The independence movement led by Gandhi won the British withdrawal in 1947, at the cost of partition with Pakistan, which displaced 15 million people and killed about a million. It is the largest democracy in the world.

360.name: Indonesia
360.fato: The largest archipelago in the world, with more than 17,000 islands, it was the center of the Srivijaya and Majapahit empires and then of the Dutch spice trade for three and a half centuries. It proclaimed independence in 1945, confirmed after four years of war. The anti-communist massacre of 1965–66 killed hundreds of thousands and brought Suharto to power for 32 years. It is the country with the most Muslims in the world.

364.name: Iran
364.fato: The Achaemenid Empire, in the 6th century BC, was the largest the world had yet seen and produced one of the first charters of rights. Persian and Zoroastrian before the Arab conquest, it adopted Shiism as its state religion in the 16th century. The 1953 coup backed by the US and the UK toppled Mossadegh, who had nationalized oil. The 1979 Revolution created the Islamic Republic.

368.name: Iraq
368.fato: Mesopotamia produced cuneiform writing, the first cities and the Code of Hammurabi. Baghdad was the intellectual center of the Islamic world until the Mongol destruction of 1258. Created by the British in 1920 by joining three Ottoman provinces. Saddam Hussein ruled from 1979 to 2003, with war against Iran, the invasion of Kuwait and, finally, the American invasion that toppled him.

372.name: Ireland
372.fato: Colonized by England from the 12th century, it suffered the Great Famine of 1845–49, which killed a million and drove as many to emigrate. The Easter Rising of 1916 and the war that followed led to independence in 1922, with the partition of the North. Neutral in World War II, the country climbed out of poverty in the 1990s through foreign investment and education.

376.name: Israel
376.fato: The Zionist movement drove Jewish immigration to Ottoman and later British Palestine, accelerated by the Holocaust. Founded in 1948, after the UN partition plan, it fought wars with Arab countries in 1948, 1967 and 1973. The occupation of Palestinian territories since 1967 and the conflict with the Palestinians remain the unresolved axis of the region.

380.name: Italy
380.fato: Center of the Roman Empire and later of the Renaissance, it remained divided into kingdoms and city-states until unification in 1861, led by Garibaldi and Piedmont. Rome was only incorporated in 1870. Mussolini's fascism ruled from 1922 to 1943, allied with Nazi Germany. The monarchy was abolished by referendum in 1946, and the country became one of the founders of the European Community.

384.name: Ivory Coast
384.fato: The "Ivory Coast" is named after the trade Europeans sought here. A French colony, it became independent in 1960 under Houphouët-Boigny, who made it the world's largest cocoa producer and moved the capital to his hometown, Yamoussoukro, where he built the largest Christian basilica in the world. It went through civil war between 2002 and 2011.

388.name: Jamaica
388.fato: Spanish and then English from 1655, it became one of the world's largest sugar producers with enslaved labor. The Maroons won autonomy by treaty as early as the 18th century. Independent in 1962. It gave the world reggae, the Rastafari movement and Bob Marley, along with enormous cultural influence.

392.name: Japan
392.fato: Ruled by shoguns and samurai for seven centuries, it closed itself off from 1639 to 1853, when American ships forced it open. The Meiji Restoration industrialized the country in one generation and made it an imperial power, expanding over Korea, China and the Pacific. Defeated in 1945, after Hiroshima and Nagasaki, it rebuilt under a pacifist constitution and became the world's second-largest economy.

398.name: Kazakhstan
398.fato: Land of steppe nomads, it was absorbed by the Russian Empire in the 19th century. Under the Soviets it suffered a devastating famine in the 1930s, received deportees of many ethnic groups, and hosted nuclear tests at Semipalatinsk and the Baikonur Cosmodrome. Independent in 1991, it is the largest landlocked country and lives off oil, gas and uranium.

400.name: Jordan
400.fato: Petra, carved into the rock, was the capital of the Nabataean kingdom. Created as the British emirate of Transjordan in 1921, independent in 1946 under the Hashemite dynasty. It controlled the West Bank until 1967. It took in successive waves of Palestinian, Iraqi and Syrian refugees, becoming one of the countries with the highest share of refugees in the world. It made peace with Israel in 1994.

404.name: Kenya
404.fato: The Rift Valley holds some of the oldest human fossils ever found. The Swahili coast traded with Arabs and Persians for a thousand years. A British colony with white settlers in the highlands, it lived through the Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s, violently suppressed. Independent in 1963 under Kenyatta. Its economy is the most diversified in East Africa.

408.name: North Korea
408.fato: Formed in the 1945 division under Soviet tutelage, it has been led by three generations of the same family since 1948. The Korean War devastated its territory under heavy bombing. It adopted the Juche doctrine of self-reliance and stayed closed while the South prospered. The famine of the 1990s killed hundreds of thousands. It developed nuclear weapons from the 2000s.

410.name: South Korea
410.fato: Korean kingdoms fought over the peninsula for a thousand years until unification under Joseon, in 1392, which created the Hangul alphabet to teach the people to read. A Japanese colony from 1910 to 1945, it was divided at the 38th parallel at the end of the war. The Korean War (1950–53) killed millions and ended in an armistice, with no peace treaty. It went from a devastated country to an industrial power in four decades, and democratized in 1987.

414.name: Kuwait
414.fato: A port and trading town founded in the 18th century, it was a British protectorate until 1961. Oil, discovered in 1938, funded a generous welfare state and the most active parliament in the Gulf. The Iraqi invasion of 1990 led to the Gulf War and liberation in 1991, with oil wells set ablaze that burned for months.

417.name: Kyrgyzstan
417.fato: A nomadic people whose Epic of Manas is one of the longest oral poems in the world. Annexed by Russia in the 19th century, with a revolt crushed in 1916. Independent in 1991, it became the most politically turbulent country in Central Asia, with three revolutions that toppled presidents in 2005, 2010 and 2020.

418.name: Laos
418.fato: The kingdom of Lan Xang, "land of a million elephants", dominated the region for four centuries. A French protectorate from 1893. Between 1964 and 1973 it became the most heavily bombed country in history, per capita, in the American secret war — unexploded bombs still kill. The Pathet Lao took power in 1975 and keeps a one-party state.

422.name: Lebanon
422.fato: From here the Phoenicians spread the alphabet across the Mediterranean. Under French mandate, it became independent in 1943 with a power-sharing system among religious communities. The civil war from 1975 to 1990 destroyed Beirut, once called the Paris of the East. It endured Israeli and Syrian occupations, and the 2020 port explosion amid a historic financial collapse.

426.name: Lesotho
426.fato: The Basotho kingdom was formed by Moshoeshoe I in the 19th century to resist the Boers and the Zulus, and asked for British protection to survive. Independent in 1966, it is the only country lying entirely above 1,000 meters and is completely surrounded by South Africa, on which it depends economically. It exports water and labor.

428.name: Latvia
428.fato: Riga, founded in 1201, was a major trading post of the Hanseatic League. The territory passed through German, Polish, Swedish and Russian hands. Independent in 1918, it was annexed by Stalin in 1940 and suffered mass deportations. The Singing Revolution and the 1989 Baltic Way human chain led to independence in 1991.

430.name: Liberia
430.fato: Founded in 1822 by freed African Americans with the support of American societies, it declared independence in 1847 — the first African republic. The Americo-Liberian elite ruled over the local peoples until the 1980 coup. Two civil wars, between 1989 and 2003, killed about 250,000 people. In 2006 it elected Africa's first female head of state.

434.name: Libya
434.fato: Leptis Magna is among the best-preserved Roman ruins in the world. An Italian colony from 1911, with brutal repression of the resistance. Independent in 1951, it found oil shortly after. Gaddafi ruled from 1969 to 2011, when he was overthrown and killed in a NATO-backed uprising. The country plunged into civil war and division.

438.name: Liechtenstein
438.fato: Bought by an Austrian family in 1719 to gain a seat in the Holy Roman Empire, the principality became independent in 1866 and disbanded its army in 1868 because it cost too much. After the war it went from a poor farming country to one of the richest in the world, with precision industry and financial services. Women could only vote from 1984.

440.name: Lithuania
440.fato: In the 14th century, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania was the largest state in Europe, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea. It was the last European country to be Christianized. Absorbed by Russia in 1795 and by the Soviet Union in 1940, it regained independence in 1990, the first Soviet republic to do so. Vilnius was known as the Jerusalem of the North before the Holocaust.

442.name: Luxembourg
442.fato: A fortress fought over for centuries, it became a grand duchy in 1815 and had its independence guaranteed in 1867, on condition that it tear down its walls. It lost more than half its territory to Belgium. Occupied in both wars, it was a founder of the ECSC in 1951, the seed of the European Union, and became a heavyweight financial center.

446.name: Macau
al: Macao Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China
Macau Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China
446.fato: It was a Portuguese trading post for more than four centuries, until 1999.

450.name: Madagascar
450.fato: Settled by Austronesian seafarers from Southeast Asia about 1,500 years ago, which explains its Malayo-Polynesian language. The Merina kingdom unified the island in the 19th century, before the French conquest in 1896. Independent in 1960. Its wildlife evolved in isolation for 88 million years, and most of its species exist nowhere else.

454.name: Malawi
454.fato: Lake Malawi holds more fish species than any other lake in the world. It was British Nyasaland, and Livingstone passed through here fighting the slave trade. Independent in 1964, it lived for thirty years under Hastings Banda's personal rule. It is one of the most densely populated and poorest countries in Africa.

458.name: Malaysia
458.fato: Malacca controlled the strait through which the spice trade passed, attracting the Portuguese, the Dutch and the British. The British brought in Chinese and Indian workers, creating today's multiethnic society. Independent in 1957, it expelled Singapore from the federation in 1965. It is one of the world's largest producers of palm oil and electronic components.

462.name: Maldives
462.fato: A trade route in the Indian Ocean, it converted to Islam in the 12th century and was a sultanate for 800 years. A British protectorate until 1965, it became a republic in 1968. Gayoom ruled for thirty years, and the first multiparty election was in 2008. With almost all its land less than two meters above sea level, it is the country most threatened by rising oceans.

466.name: Mali
466.fato: Timbuktu and Djenné were centers of Islamic learning and of the gold and salt trade in the Mali Empire, which in the 14th century was one of the richest in the world. A French colony until 1960. Since 2012 it has faced a Tuareg rebellion in the north and the spread of jihadist groups, with French and later Russian intervention.

470.name: Malta
470.fato: Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs and Normans all passed through. It was handed to the Knights of Malta in 1530, who withstood the Ottoman Great Siege of 1565. British from 1800, it became a key base in the Mediterranean and suffered brutal bombing in World War II. Independent in 1964.

474.name: Martinique
474.fato: The eruption of Mount Pelée, in 1902, destroyed Saint-Pierre.

478.name: Mauritania
478.fato: A bridge between the Arab-Berber Maghreb and sub-Saharan Africa, with a strong nomadic heritage. Independent from France in 1960. It was the last country in the world to formally abolish slavery, in 1981, and only criminalized it in 2007 — the practice persists. It disputed Western Sahara in the 1970s and mines iron ore.

480.name: Mauritius
480.fato: Uninhabited until the Europeans arrived; the dodo, found only here, went extinct in the 17th century. The Dutch, French and British colonized it, bringing enslaved Africans and later Indian workers — the origin of most of the population. Independent in 1968, it went from a sugar monoculture to a diversified economy, with the highest HDI in Africa.

484.name: Mexico
484.fato: Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, was one of the largest cities in the world when Cortés destroyed it in 1521. Three centuries of viceroyalty ended with independence in 1821. It lost half its territory to the US in 1848. The Revolution of 1910 redistributed land and shaped the modern state, ruled by the same party for 71 years.

492.name: Monaco
492.fato: The Grimaldis seized the fortress in 1297 and have ruled ever since, the longest-lasting dynasty in Europe. It lost most of its territory in 1861 by selling Menton and Roquebrune to France. The Monte Carlo casino, opened in 1863, saved the principality from bankruptcy and defined its identity. It levies no personal income tax.

496.name: Mongolia
496.fato: Genghis Khan united the tribes in 1206 and created the largest contiguous empire in history, stretching from Korea to Hungary. Later absorbed by Qing China, it became independent in 1921 with Soviet support and was the world's second communist state. It made a peaceful transition to democracy in 1990. It is the least densely populated country on the planet.

498.name: Moldova
498.fato: Bessarabia went from Ottoman to Russian rule in 1812, joined Romania in 1918 and was annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940. Independent in 1991, it saw the Transnistria region break away de facto after a brief war in 1992, with Russian support. It is one of the poorest countries in Europe, with heavy emigration.

499.name: Montenegro
499.fato: It kept relative autonomy even under the Ottomans, ruled by prince-bishops. An independent kingdom in 1878, it was absorbed by Yugoslavia. It stayed united with Serbia until 2006, when a close referendum restored its independence, without violence. It adopted the euro without being part of the eurozone.

504.name: Morocco
504.fato: It was the first country to recognize the independence of the United States, in 1777. Successive Berber and Arab dynasties have ruled since the 8th century; the current one has reigned since 1666. A French and Spanish protectorate from 1912 to 1956. It annexed Western Sahara in 1975, where the conflict with the Polisario Front remains without a final solution.

508.name: Mozambique
508.fato: Mozambique Island was the capital of Portuguese East Africa and a stop on the route to the Indies. FRELIMO fought for independence, won in 1975, and the country plunged into a civil war with RENAMO, backed by Rhodesia and South Africa, which lasted until 1992 and killed a million people. Since 2017 it has faced an insurgency in the north, near large gas reserves.

512.name: Oman
512.fato: A maritime empire that controlled Zanzibar and part of the East African coast until the 19th century, with a strong naval tradition. A longtime ally of the British. In 1970 Sultan Qaboos deposed his father and pulled the country out of extreme isolation, building schools, roads and hospitals within a few decades. It keeps a foreign policy of regional mediation.

516.name: Namibia
516.fato: A German colony where the genocide of the Herero and Nama took place between 1904 and 1908, considered the first of the 20th century. Administered by South Africa after World War I, it had apartheid extended to its territory. After SWAPO's long struggle, it only became independent in 1990, one of the last in Africa. It is home to the oldest desert in the world.

520.name: Nauru
520.fato: One of the world's largest phosphate reserves, mined by Germans, British and Australians, gave the country one of the highest per capita incomes on the planet in the 1970s. The depletion of the reserve and mismanaged investments led to collapse, leaving 80% of the land uninhabitable. It came to live off Australia's migrant detention centers.

524.name: Nepal
524.fato: Unified in the 18th century by the Shah dynasty, it was never colonized, although it ceded territory to the British. The Gurkhas won worldwide military fame. It went through a Maoist civil war between 1996 and 2006, and the monarchy ended in 2008, after the massacre of the royal family in 2001, becoming a republic. It is home to eight of the fourteen peaks above 8,000 meters.

528.name: Netherlands
528.fato: It rebelled against Spain in 1568, in an eighty-year war. In the 17th century it lived through its Golden Age: the East India Company, the first publicly traded company, and global commercial dominance. It lost New Amsterdam to the English in 1667 and Indonesia in 1949. Much of its land was won from the sea with dikes and polders.

531.name: Curaçao
531.fato: It was the center of Dutch trade in the Caribbean.

533.name: Aruba
533.fato: It left the Netherlands Antilles in 1986 to get a status of its own.

540.name: New Caledonia
al: Territory of New Caledonia and Dependencies
540.fato: A French territory in the Pacific, with a strong presence of the Kanak people.

548.name: Vanuatu
548.fato: Governed jointly by France and the United Kingdom in a condominium rare in colonial history, with two parallel legal systems, until independence in 1980. It preserves a strong kastom culture and more than a hundred languages for a small population. It is among the countries at highest risk of natural disasters in the world.

554.name: New Zealand
554.fato: Settled by Polynesians around 1300, who created Māori culture. The Treaty of Waitangi, of 1840, formalized British sovereignty and still governs the relationship with the Māori, with disputes over its interpretation to this day. It was the first country in the world to give women the vote, in 1893. It declared itself a nuclear-free zone in 1987.

558.name: Nicaragua
558.fato: Fought over as an interoceanic route alternative to Panama. Occupied by US Marines between 1912 and 1933, it resisted with Sandino. The Somoza dynasty ruled until the Sandinista revolution of 1979, followed by the war against the US-funded Contras. Daniel Ortega returned to power in 2007 and remains there.

562.name: Niger
562.fato: Agadez was a central hub of the trans-Saharan caravans. Independent from France in 1960. It suffers from recurring droughts, Tuareg revolts and, more recently, jihadist attacks in the Sahel. It is a major uranium producer, yet remains among the lowest-income countries in the world, with the highest fertility rate on the planet.

566.name: Nigeria
566.fato: It was home to the bronzes of the Kingdom of Benin and to the Sokoto and Kanem caliphates. Artificially unified by the British in 1914, joining the Muslim north and the Christian south. Independent in 1960, it went through the Biafran War (1967–70), with more than a million dead, and decades of military rule. It is the most populous country in Africa and the continent's largest oil producer.

578.name: Norway
578.fato: A Viking cradle, it was united with Denmark for four centuries and later with Sweden, from which it separated peacefully by referendum in 1905. Occupied by the Nazis from 1940 to 1945. The discovery of North Sea oil, in 1969, transformed the country and created the largest sovereign wealth fund on the planet. It rejected joining the European Union in two referendums.

580.name: Northern Mariana Islands
al: Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands
Commonwealth of the Northern Maria Islands

583.name: Micronesia
583.fato: Nan Madol, on Pohnpei, is a stone city built on reefs between the 13th and 17th centuries, a feat of engineering unique in the Pacific. It passed through Spanish, German and Japanese hands, then American administration. Independent in 1986, it keeps a free association with the US.

584.name: Marshall Islands
584.fato: Bikini and Enewetak atolls were used for 67 American nuclear tests between 1946 and 1958, including the Castle Bravo bomb — whole populations were displaced and still cannot return. Independent in 1986 in free association with the US. Today it faces the direct threat of sea-level rise.

585.name: Palau
585.fato: Inhabited for thousands of years, it passed through Spanish, German and Japanese hands and American administration. Scene of the Battle of Peleliu in 1944. Independent in 1994, it keeps a free association agreement with the United States. In 2015 it created one of the largest marine sanctuaries on the planet, protecting 80% of its waters.

586.name: Pakistan
586.fato: Heir to the Indus Valley and centuries of Mughal rule, it was created in 1947 as a state for the Muslims of British India. It lost its eastern half in 1971, when Bangladesh broke away after a war. It has alternated between civilian and military governments, with four coups. It has disputed Kashmir with India since 1947, and both became nuclear powers in 1998.

591.name: Panama
591.fato: Part of Colombia until 1903, when it broke away with the support of the US, which wanted the canal. The canal, completed in 1914, stayed under American control until 1999, with the Canal Zone working as an enclave. Noriega was ousted by an American invasion in 1989. The canal and the financial sector sustain the economy.

598.name: Papua New Guinea
al: Independent State of Papua New Guinea
598.fato: It brings together more than 800 languages, the greatest linguistic diversity on the planet, with farming practiced in the highlands for 9,000 years. Divided between Germans and British, it passed to Australia and became independent in 1975. The civil war on Bougainville, tied to a copper mine, lasted from 1988 to 1998 and is heading toward the island's independence.

600.name: Paraguay
600.fato: Independent in 1811, it was ruled by isolationist regimes that industrialized early. The War of the Triple Alliance (1864–70) devastated it: it lost territory and much of its male population. It regained land in the Chaco War against Bolivia in the 1930s. Stroessner ruled for 35 years, until 1989. Guarani is an official language alongside Spanish.

604.name: Peru
604.fato: Cusco was the capital of the Inca Empire, the largest in pre-Columbian America, toppled by Pizarro in 1533. The Viceroyalty of Peru was the center of Spanish power in South America. Independent in 1821. It suffered the conflict with the Shining Path in the 1980s–90s, with tens of thousands dead, and Fujimori's authoritarian regime.

608.name: Philippines
608.fato: A Spanish colony for 333 years, which made it the most Catholic country in Asia, it passed to the United States in 1898 after a brief independent republic. Occupied by the Japanese and independent in 1946. Marcos ruled under martial law until he was overthrown by the People Power Revolution in 1986, a peaceful uprising that became a model worldwide.

612.name: Pitcairn Islands
al: Pitcairn, Henderson, Ducie and Oeno Islands

616.name: Poland
616.fato: The union with Lithuania created one of the largest states in Europe in the 16th century. It was partitioned among Russia, Prussia and Austria and vanished from the map from 1795 to 1918. The German invasion of 1939 opened World War II; it lost about a sixth of its population, including almost all its Jews. The Solidarity trade union, in the 1980s, opened the first crack in the Soviet bloc.

620.name: Portugal
620.fato: An autonomous county in 1128 and a kingdom in 1143, it settled its borders as early as 1249 — among the oldest in Europe. Between 1415 and 1500 it led the maritime expansion, reaching India with Vasco da Gama and Brazil with Cabral. It lost its independence to Spain between 1580 and 1640, and the monarchy fell in 1910. Salazar's dictatorship lasted from 1933 until the Carnation Revolution of 1974, which opened the way to democracy and African decolonization.

624.name: Guinea-Bissau
624.fato: Linked to the Mali Empire and later to Portuguese trade. The war of independence, led by Amílcar Cabral, was one of the most successful in Africa and helped bring down the Portuguese regime in 1974. Since independence it has piled up coups and chronic instability, made worse by international drug trafficking.

626.name: Timor-Leste
626.fato: A Portuguese colony for four centuries, it declared independence in 1975 and was invaded by Indonesia days later. The occupation, until 1999, killed about a quarter of the population. After a referendum and militia violence, it went through UN administration and became fully independent in 2002, the first new country of the 21st century.

630.name: Puerto Rico
al: Free Associated State of Puerto Rico
630.fato: A US territory since 1898; its inhabitants are American citizens.

634.name: Qatar
634.fato: A pearl-fishing village under Ottoman rule and then a British protectorate, independent in 1971. Tapping the world's largest natural gas field, from the 1990s, gave it one of the highest per capita incomes on the planet. It founded Al Jazeera in 1996 and hosted the 2022 World Cup, criticized for the conditions of migrant workers.

638.name: Réunion
638.fato: A French volcanic island in the Indian Ocean, uninhabited until the 17th century.

642.name: Romania
642.fato: Formed by the union of Wallachia and Moldavia in 1859, it inherited its Latin character from ancient Roman Dacia. It gained Transylvania after World War I. It allied with the Axis and then switched sides in 1944. Ceaușescu's regime, marked by surveillance and shortages, ended with his execution in the 1989 revolution, the only violent one in the Soviet bloc.

643.name: Russia
643.fato: Born from Kievan Rus', it paid tribute to the Mongols for two centuries and grew out of Moscow until it became the largest country in the world. Peter the Great Europeanized the state; the tsars fell in the Revolution of 1917. The Soviet Union defeated Nazi Germany at the cost of 27 million dead and fought the Cold War with the US, until it dissolved in 1991.

646.name: Rwanda
al: The Land of a Thousand Hills
646.fato: A centralized kingdom before German and Belgian colonization, which hardened the Hutu–Tutsi divide in order to rule. Independent in 1962, it went through recurring massacres. In 1994 the genocide killed about 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in a hundred days, amid international inaction. Since then it has rebuilt with rapid growth under Kagame's authoritarian government.

654.name: Saint Helena
al: Saint Helena, Ascension, and Tristan da Cunha
Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
654.fato: The island where Napoleon was exiled in 1815 and died in 1821. It was a way station of the East India Company.

659.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
al: Federation of Saint Christopher and Nevis
Federation of Saint Kitts and Nevis
659.fato: The first English and then French colony in the eastern Caribbean, it was called the "mother colony" of the West Indies. Independent in 1983, it is the smallest country in the Americas by area and population. It shut down its sugar industry in 2005 and shifted to tourism and services.

662.name: Saint Lucia
662.fato: It changed hands between France and England fourteen times, earning it the nickname Helen of the West Indies. Independent in 1979. Tiny as it is, it has produced two Nobel laureates — Arthur Lewis, in economics, and Derek Walcott, in literature.

666.name: Saint Pierre and Miquelon
al: Territorial Collectivity of Saint Pierre and Miquelon

670.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
670.fato: The last Caribbean island to be effectively colonized, thanks to the resistance of the Black Caribs, deported en masse by the British in 1797. Independent in 1979. Eruptions of the La Soufrière volcano have forced mass evacuations more than once, including in 2021.

674.name: San Marino
al: Most Serene Republic of San Marino
674.fato: Tradition dates its founding to 301, which makes it the oldest republic in the world. It survived Italian unification because it had sheltered Garibaldi. It stayed neutral in World War II and took in more than 100,000 refugees, several times its population. Its constitution, of 1600, is among the oldest still in force.

678.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
al: Democratic Republic of São Tomé and Príncipe
678.fato: Uninhabited islands occupied by Portugal in the 15th century, they were among the world's first sugar plantations worked by enslaved people — a model later exported to the Americas. In the early 20th century it was the world's largest cocoa producer, with forced labor that caused an international scandal. Independent in 1975.

682.name: Saudi Arabia
682.fato: The alliance between the House of Saud and the preacher Abd al-Wahhab, in the 18th century, defined the state. The current kingdom was unified in 1932. The discovery of oil in 1938 made it the world's greatest energy power. It holds Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities of Islam. Since 2017 it has pushed rapid social change under strict political control.

686.name: Senegal
686.fato: Gorée Island was a hub of the Atlantic slave trade and is now a memorial. The center of French West Africa, it had deputies in the French parliament before independence, in 1960. Léopold Senghor, poet and theorist of Négritude, ruled for twenty years and stepped down voluntarily. It is one of the few African countries that have never had a coup.

688.name: Serbia
688.fato: The medieval Serbian empire collapsed at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, a landmark of its national identity. Autonomous from the Ottomans in the 19th century, it led the creation of Yugoslavia in 1918. Under Milošević it was at the center of the wars of the 1990s; NATO's 1999 bombing led to the loss of control over Kosovo. Belgrade has been destroyed and rebuilt dozens of times.

690.name: Seychelles
690.fato: An archipelago uninhabited until the 18th century, colonized by the French with enslaved people and later taken by the British. Independent in 1976, it had a socialist coup the following year and one-party rule until 1993. It has the smallest territory and population in Africa, the highest HDI on the continent, and protects almost half its land.

694.name: Sierra Leone
694.fato: Freetown was created in 1787 as a colony for freed enslaved people. British until 1961. The civil war from 1991 to 2002, funded by conflict diamonds, was marked by mutilations and child soldiers. It was also hit by the 2014 Ebola outbreak. It rebuilt its institutions with international support.

702.name: Singapore
702.fato: Founded as a British trading post by Raffles in 1819, it became the busiest port in Asia. Occupied by the Japanese in World War II. Expelled from Malaysia in 1965, with no natural resources and ethnic tensions, it bet on education, ports, industry and finance under Lee Kuan Yew, going from a poor country to one of the richest in the world in one generation.

703.name: Slovakia
703.fato: Ruled by Hungary for a thousand years, it joined Czechoslovakia in 1918. It was a Nazi satellite state between 1939 and 1945. After 1989 and the Velvet Revolution, it separated peacefully from the Czechs in 1993, the so-called Velvet Divorce. It industrialized quickly and adopted the euro in 2009.

704.name: Vietnam
704.fato: It resisted a thousand years of Chinese domination before securing its independence in the 10th century. A French colony from the 19th century, it drove the French out at Dien Bien Phu in 1954 and was divided. The Vietnam War, with American intervention, ended in 1975 with reunification. The Đổi Mới reforms of 1986 opened the economy and produced rapid growth.

705.name: Slovenia
705.fato: Under Austrian rule for six centuries, it preserved the Slovene language through literature. It was the most prosperous region of Yugoslavia. Its exit, in 1991, cost only ten days of fighting — by far the least violent separation in the Yugoslav breakup. It joined the European Union and the euro quickly.

706.name: Somalia
706.fato: Land of trading sultanates on the Indian Ocean route, it was divided between the British and the Italians and reunified at independence, in 1960. The fall of Siad Barre, in 1991, dissolved the central state: clan warfare, famine, a failed American intervention in 1993 and the rise of al-Shabaab followed. Somaliland declared an unrecognized independence.

710.name: South Africa
710.fato: Colonized by the Dutch and the British, it saw the Boer Wars and the discovery of gold and diamonds shape its state. Apartheid, institutionalized in 1948, legally segregated the Black majority for four decades. Mandela spent 27 years in prison and was elected president in 1994, in the first free elections, with a Truth Commission instead of revenge.

716.name: Zimbabwe
716.fato: Great Zimbabwe, a stone city built between the 11th and 15th centuries, was the capital of an African trading empire. Colonized by Cecil Rhodes, it became Rhodesia, which declared independence under white minority rule in 1965. After a liberation war it became Zimbabwe in 1980 under Mugabe, who ruled for 37 years; the land reform of the 2000s and hyperinflation destroyed the economy.

724.name: Spain
724.fato: Eight centuries of Muslim presence ended in 1492, the same year it funded Columbus's voyage. The union of Castile and Aragon formed an empire that drew silver from the Americas and dominated Europe in the 16th century. Decline came with successive wars; the American colonies broke free between 1810 and 1825. The Civil War of 1936–39 brought Franco to power for almost forty years, and democracy only returned in 1978.

728.name: South Sudan
728.fato: Marginalized under Anglo-Egyptian rule and then by the government in Khartoum, it fought two civil wars that add up to almost fifty years. A 2005 peace agreement led to the 2011 referendum, in which almost 99% voted to separate — making it the world's newest country. Two years later it plunged into a civil war of its own.

729.name: Sudan
729.fato: The Kingdom of Kush, at Meroë, once ruled Egypt and built more pyramids than the Egyptians. Anglo-Egyptian from 1899, independent in 1956. It went through two long civil wars between north and south, the Darfur conflict from 2003 and the separation of South Sudan in 2011. Bashir fell in 2019, and war between military factions broke out again in 2023.

732.name: Western Sahara
732.fato: A non-self-governing territory whose final status is still in dispute.

740.name: Suriname
740.fato: Traded by the English for New Amsterdam, the future New York, in 1667. Under the Dutch it had a plantation economy with enslaved labor; runaway communities formed the Maroon peoples, who survive to this day. Indian and Javanese workers arrived later. Independent in 1975, it went through a military coup and civil war in the 1980s.

748.name: Eswatini
748.fato: A kingdom consolidated in the 19th century, it became a British protectorate and regained independence in 1968. It is Africa's last absolute monarchy: political parties were banned in 1973. It changed its name from Swaziland to Eswatini in 2018. It has faced one of the highest HIV rates in the world and pro-democracy protests in 2021.

752.name: Sweden
752.fato: A military power of the Baltic in the 17th century under Gustavus Adolphus, it lost that position to Russia in 1721. It has not been at war since 1814, Europe's record for continuous peace. It stayed neutral in both world wars. In the 20th century it built one of the most extensive welfare states in the world, and gave up non-alignment when it joined NATO in 2024.

756.name: Switzerland
756.fato: It was born from a mutual defense pact between three cantons in 1291. After centuries of supplying mercenaries to Europe, it adopted permanent neutrality in 1815, kept through both world wars. Its direct democracy often puts laws to referendum; federal women's suffrage, however, only came in 1971. Home of the Red Cross since 1863.

760.name: Syria
760.fato: Damascus is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and was the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate, which stretched from Spain to India. Under French mandate after the Ottoman collapse, independent in 1946. The Assad family ruled from 1971 to 2024. The crackdown on the 2011 protests set off a civil war with half a million dead and millions of refugees.

762.name: Tajikistan
762.fato: Heir to Persian culture in Central Asia, with Samarkand and Bukhara historically Tajik before ending up in Uzbekistan. Soviet from the 1920s. After independence, in 1991, it went through a five-year civil war with tens of thousands dead. It is the most mountainous country in the region and depends heavily on emigrants' remittances.

764.name: Thailand
764.fato: Successor to the Sukhothai and Ayutthaya kingdoms, it is the only country in Southeast Asia never colonized, thanks to diplomacy between the British and the French. The absolute monarchy ended in 1932. Since then it has piled up more than a dozen military coups. It allied with the US in the Cold War and built one of the largest tourism industries in the world.

768.name: Togo
768.fato: A German colony until World War I, it was split between France and the United Kingdom. Independent in 1960. The Gnassingbé family has ruled since 1967, one of the longest stays in power in the world. Its economy depends on phosphate, cotton and the port of Lomé.

776.name: Tonga
776.fato: The only Pacific country that never lost its sovereignty: it negotiated British protection in 1900 without becoming a colony and regained full autonomy in 1970. The monarchy goes back a thousand years. It moved from a near-absolute monarchy to democratic reforms in 2010. In 2022 it suffered the most violent volcanic eruption recorded in decades.

780.name: Trinidad and Tobago
780.fato: Spanish and then British, it took in indentured Indian workers after abolition, forming a society divided between people of African and of Indian descent. Independent in 1962. Oil and gas made it one of the richest economies in the Caribbean. Its carnival gave birth to calypso, soca and the steelpan.

784.name: United Arab Emirates
784.fato: The Pirate Coast to the British, it lived off pearl diving until that market collapsed in the 1930s. Seven emirates formed the federation in 1971, after the British withdrawal. Abu Dhabi's oil funded a dizzying transformation; Dubai bet on trade, tourism and finance. Today more than 80% of the population is foreign.

788.name: Tunisia
788.fato: Carthage rivaled Rome in the Punic Wars until it was razed in 146 BC. Arab from the 7th century and later Ottoman, it became a French protectorate in 1881. Independent in 1956 under Bourguiba, who created the most advanced family code in the Arab world. It was where the Arab Spring began, in 2010, and the only country in the region to consolidate a democratic transition.

792.name: Turkey
792.fato: Istanbul, formerly Constantinople, was the capital of the Byzantine and Ottoman empires. The Ottomans ruled three continents for six centuries, until their collapse in World War I. Atatürk founded the republic in 1923, secular and Westernizing, replacing the alphabet and the laws. It joined NATO in 1952. The late Ottoman period includes the Armenian genocide, still not officially recognized.

795.name: Turkmenistan
795.fato: Merv was once one of the largest cities in the world, in the 12th century, before being razed by the Mongols. Land of Turkmen tribes, it was the last region the Russians conquered in Central Asia. Independent in 1991, it lived under Niyazov's personality cult, which renamed months of the calendar. It has one of the largest gas reserves in the world.

798.name: Tuvalu
798.fato: The former Ellice Islands split from the Gilberts by referendum and became independent in 1978. With nine atolls and a maximum elevation of a few meters, it is one of the countries most vulnerable to rising seas — and has begun archiving its culture digitally. It earns significant revenue by leasing its internet domain, .tv.

800.name: Uganda
800.fato: It brought together powerful kingdoms, such as Buganda, before the British protectorate. Independent in 1962. Idi Amin ruled from 1971 to 1979, expelled the Asian community and left hundreds of thousands dead. Civil war followed and, in the north, decades of conflict with the Lord's Resistance Army. Museveni has ruled since 1986.

804.name: Ukraine
804.fato: Kievan Rus', from the 9th century, is the shared historical root of Ukrainians and Russians. Divided among Poles, Ottomans and Russians, it lived through the Holodomor of 1932–33, an engineered famine that killed millions. Independent in 1991, it gave up its nuclear arsenal in 1994. The 2014 Revolution was followed by the annexation of Crimea and, in 2022, by the full-scale Russian invasion.

807.name: North Macedonia
807.fato: A territory contested by Greeks, Bulgarians and Serbs, it left Yugoslavia in 1991 without war. It spent almost three decades in a diplomatic standoff with Greece over its name, resolved in 2019 by adopting "North Macedonia" — which unlocked its entry into NATO. It has a large Albanian minority, whose tensions nearly turned into war in 2001.

818.name: Egypt
818.fato: The pyramids of Giza were already two thousand years old when Rome was founded. After pharaohs, Greeks and Romans, it was Arabized in the 7th century and Ottoman from 1517. The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, drew British occupation. The 1952 revolution toppled the monarchy; Nasser nationalized the canal in 1956. The Arab Spring overthrew Mubarak in 2011.

826.name: United Kingdom
al: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
826.fato: The union of England and Scotland created the United Kingdom in 1707. It pioneered the Industrial Revolution and came to rule a quarter of the planet, the largest empire in history. Ireland broke away in 1922. Two world wars drained its resources, and decolonization dismantled the empire between 1947 and 1970. It left the European Union in 2020, after the 2016 referendum.

832.name: Jersey
832.fato: The last part of the Duchy of Normandy still tied to the British Crown.

833.name: Isle of Man
833.fato: Tynwald, its parliament, claims more than a thousand years of operation.

834.name: Tanzania
al: United Republic of Tanganyika and Zanzibar
834.fato: Zanzibar was a center of the slave and spice trade in the Indian Ocean. A German and then British colony, the mainland became Tanganyika, independent in 1961, and united with Zanzibar in 1964. Nyerere applied the African socialism of Ujamaa, with poor economic results but strong national cohesion. It is home to the Serengeti and Kilimanjaro.

840.name: United States
840.fato: Thirteen British colonies declared independence in 1776; the 1787 constitution is still in force, the oldest in the world. It expanded west at the expense of Native peoples and Mexico. The Civil War (1861–65) abolished slavery, but segregation lasted until the 1960s. It emerged from the two world wars as a superpower and led the West in the Cold War.

850.name: United States Virgin Islands
al: Virgin Islands of the United States
850.fato: Bought by the US from Denmark in 1917.

854.name: Burkina Faso
854.fato: The Mossi kingdoms resisted invaders for centuries. The colony of Upper Volta adopted its current name, "land of upright people", in 1984 under Thomas Sankara, who pushed radical reforms before being assassinated in 1987. Compaoré ruled for 27 years until he was toppled by a popular uprising in 2014. It suffers from jihadist violence in the Sahel.

858.name: Uruguay
858.fato: Fought over by the Spanish and the Portuguese, it was a province of Brazil before becoming independent in 1828 as a buffer state. In the early 20th century, under Batlle y Ordóñez, it built one of the first welfare states in the Americas. It lived under dictatorship from 1973 to 1985. It was the first country in the world to legalize the cannabis market, in 2013.

860.name: Uzbekistan
860.fato: Samarkand and Bukhara were hubs of the Silk Road and centers of Islamic science; Tamerlane made Samarkand his capital in the 14th century. Conquered by Russia in the 19th century, it was a Soviet republic until 1991. Soviet cotton farming drained the Aral Sea, one of the greatest environmental disasters of the 20th century.

862.name: Venezuela
862.fato: Named by navigators who compared Indigenous stilt houses to Venice. Birthplace of Simón Bolívar, liberator of five countries. The discovery of oil in the 1920s made it the richest country in the region. Chávez came to power in 1999 and launched chavismo; the fall in oil prices and the crisis from 2014 caused one of the largest exoduses in the world.

882.name: Samoa
882.fato: Fought over by Germans, British and Americans in the 19th century, it became a German and then a New Zealand colony — whose administration let the 1918 flu kill a fifth of the population. The Mau movement resisted peacefully and won, in 1962, the first independence of a Pacific island nation.

887.name: Yemen
887.fato: The kingdom of Saba, of the legendary Queen of Sheba, prospered here on the incense trade. Divided between north and south until unification in 1990. The civil war that began in 2014, with Saudi intervention, produced one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world. It is the poorest country on the Arabian Peninsula, despite its history of commercial wealth.

894.name: Zambia
894.fato: Victoria Falls, on the Zambezi, are among the largest in the world. It was British Northern Rhodesia, exploited for its Copperbelt. Independent in 1964 under Kaunda, who ruled for 27 years and backed neighboring liberation movements. It has made peaceful transfers of power through elections since the 1990s.

926.name: Kosovo
926.fato: An Albanian-majority Serbian province, it was the scene of the 1389 battle that became a Serbian national symbol. The repression of the 1990s and the 1998–99 war ended with NATO bombing and UN administration. It declared independence in 2008, recognized by much of the West, but not by Serbia, Russia or China.

gb-eng.name: England
gb-eng.fato: Unified in the 10th century, it gave rise to the state that would colonize a quarter of the planet. The St George's Cross comes from the Crusades.

gb-sct.name: Scotland
gb-sct.fato: An independent kingdom until 1707, when it united with England. It rejected separation in a 2014 referendum by 55% to 45%.

gb-wls.name: Wales
gb-wls.fato: Annexed by England in 1284. Its flag, with the red dragon, is the only one in the United Kingdom missing from the Union Jack.

gb-nir.name: Northern Ireland
gb-nir.fato: Created in 1921 with the partition of Ireland. The conflict known as the Troubles lasted until the Good Friday Agreement, in 1998.

sh-ac.name: Ascension Island
sh-ac.fato: A volcanic island occupied by the British in 1815 to keep watch on Napoleon. It served as an air base in World War II and in the Falklands War.

sh-ta.name: Tristan da Cunha
sh-ta.fato: The most remote inhabited archipelago in the world, 2,400 km from the nearest land. It was entirely evacuated because of an eruption in 1961.

bq-se.name: Sint Eustatius
bq-se.fato: It was the busiest port in the Caribbean in the 18th century, nicknamed the Golden Rock, and the first foreign territory to salute the flag of the United States, in 1776. It lost its importance after the British sack of 1781.

cl-ip.name: Easter Island
al: Te pito o te kainga a Hau Maka
cl-ip.fato: Settled by Polynesians around the year 1200, it raised almost a thousand moai in three centuries. Ecological collapse and Peruvian slave raids reduced the population to little more than a hundred people in the 19th century. Annexed by Chile in 1888.

eu.name: European Union
eu.fato: It was born from the ECSC in 1951, created to make another war between France and Germany unthinkable. The common market came in 1957 and political union with Maastricht, in 1993. It reached 28 members before the British exit in 2020.

xa.name: Abkhazia
xa.fato: A medieval kingdom in its own right, it was absorbed by Georgia under Russian rule and became a Soviet autonomous republic. The 1992–93 war drove out much of the Georgian population and created a de facto state, recognized by Russia after the 2008 conflict and by very few other countries.

xo.name: South Ossetia
al: Republic of South Ossetia – the State of Alania
xo.fato: Separated from North Ossetia, which stayed in Russia, it declared independence in 1990 and fought Georgia in two wars. Since 2008 it has lived under Russian military presence, with almost no international recognition. Its flag repeats the colors of the Ossetian people on both sides of the Caucasus.

bat.name: British Antarctic Territory
bat.fato: A British claim south of the 60th parallel, created in 1962 and overlapping the claims of Chile and Argentina. The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 froze all of them: no one recognizes them, no one gives them up. Its population is a few hundred researchers in summer.
